blocks.text: 07: WHAT EXACTLY WAS MARY RISKING WHEN SHE SAID YES?

sentences: The answer Gabriel gives to Mary in Luke chapter one, verse thirty-one, is brief.
You'll conceive and give birth to a son.
Eleven words in English.

What those eleven words meant for a teenage girl in first-century Judea, given the specific social and legal circumstances she was standing inside of, is something most modern readers pass over without recognition.
Understanding what Mary was risking when she said yes isn't a devotional exercise.
It's an evidentiary one.
Mary was betrothed to Joseph.
That phrase, in our cultural context, sounds roughly equivalent to engaged, and we tend to read it that way, with the assumptions of modern Western engagement attached.
A couple is committed, their families approve, they wear matching jewelry, and the wedding is on the calendar.
A betrothed woman in first-century Jewish culture was in an entirely different legal situation.
Hebrew marriage in this period was a two-stage process.
In the first stage, the two families negotiated a contractual agreement.
The groom's family paid a bride price, called the mohar, to the family of the bride, compensating them for the labor and household contribution of the daughter they were giving up.
Once the bride price was paid and the agreement was sealed, the couple exchanged vows in a ceremony.
They were, from that moment, legally married in the eyes of both Jewish law and their community.
What they weren't yet doing was living together.
After the vows and the payment, the bride returned to her father's house.
The groom returned to his family's property and spent the following year building the home where they would live together.
At the end of that year, a second ceremony formalized the completion of the marriage, and the bride moved to the groom's household.
The period between the two ceremonies is what Luke calls the betrothal.
It wasn't a trial period, not an engagement, not a provisional arrangement.
It was a legally binding marriage in every sense except cohabitation.
The legal consequence of that distinction is the one that matters here.
Any sexual contact between a betrothed woman and a man who wasn't her husband was treated under Deuteronomy chapter twenty-two as adultery.
The penalty for adultery was death.
A betrothed woman who became pregnant by another man faced a capital charge.

The fact that first-century Jewish communities were operating under Roman authority and that Jews didn't have the autonomous legal power to carry out executions doesn't change what the law said or what the social consequences of the accusation would be.
Joseph's response when he discovered the pregnancy tells us exactly what the community expected to happen.
He resolved to divorce her quietly, and the text notes that this was his merciful choice, because the law gave him the right to expose her to public disgrace.
Mary was no more than fifteen years old.
She was legally married.
She wasn't yet living with her husband.
When Gabriel told her she would conceive, she understood what it meant to be pregnant outside of the conditions her community recognized as legitimate.
She knew what people would say.
She knew what the law permitted.
She knew Joseph didn't yet know what was happening, and she couldn't control how he would respond.
The angel had told her.
Nobody else had.
Mary's response to Gabriel is recorded in Luke chapter one, verse thirty-eight.
I am the Lord's servant.
May your word to me be fulfilled.
That's Mary saying yes.
She isn't agreeing to an inconvenience.
She isn't accepting a difficult assignment she can manage with sufficient social support.
She's agreeing to become visibly pregnant by means she can't explain to any human being who will see her over the next nine months.
She's agreeing to carry a child her husband will immediately know isn't his, with every social and legal consequence that follow from that knowledge.
She's agreeing before Joseph has been told anything.

She's agreeing knowing that the story she will have to tell, angel came to me, Holy Spirit overshadowed me, this child is God's, is precisely the story a woman who had been unfaithful would be expected to fabricate.
Her question to Gabriel isn't a question of doubt.
It's a question of mechanism: how will this be, since I'm a virgin?
That question shows she understood her own biology.
She wasn't confused about what pregnancy required.
She was asking how the thing Gabriel was describing could happen to someone in her specific situation.
Gabriel answers.
The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.

He points her toward the impossible, uses her cousin Elizabeth's improbable pregnancy as supporting evidence that God operates outside of biological constraints, and closes with: no word from God will ever fail.
Mary says yes.
Now consider the evidentiary weight of this scene for the question of whether the story was fabricated.

A woman in the first century who wanted to construct a story to explain an illegitimate pregnancy would need to invent something that deflected blame and provided a socially defensible account of how she came to be in her situation.
The story she would most want to tell isn't this one.
This story doesn't deflect blame.
It doesn't provide a socially defensible account.
It's exactly the kind of story her community would view with maximum suspicion, because it's precisely what a woman who had been unfaithful would be expected to say.
The point sharpens when we consider what a first-century Jewish writer constructing a fictional origin story for a messianic movement would choose as his central female character.
He wouldn't choose a young betrothed woman whose pregnancy placed her under Deuteronomy chapter twenty-two.
He wouldn't give his story a central figure whose situation required an angelic visitation to prevent a capital accusation.
He wouldn't create a scenario in which the mother of the Messiah had to explain herself to a husband who had every legal and moral right to end the marriage and seek her disgrace.
No one invents the version of events that puts the central figure in the most legally and socially precarious position available.

The scenario in the Christmas story is the most dangerous possible situation for Mary, and the most inconvenient possible situation for anyone trying to invent a respectable origin story for a religious movement.

It's exactly the scenario we'd expect if something happened to Mary that she didn't engineer and couldn't explain away, and that required the direct intervention of God to prevent the consequences the law prescribed.
Mary said yes to something that could have destroyed her.
The record of that yes, preserved in detail across two independent gospel accounts, doesn't read like invention.
It reads like testimony.
The betrothal in first-century Jewish culture was a legal marriage in every dimension except cohabitation.
Mary's pregnancy under those conditions wasn't socially awkward.
It was legally actionable.
What does the decision to include that specific legal context tell us about whether the gospel writers were trying to make this story easy to believe?
Mary's question to Gabriel, how will this be since I'm a virgin, demonstrates that she understood the biological requirements of pregnancy.
She wasn't naive about what she was agreeing to.
What does it mean that she said yes anyway, with full awareness of what the community around her would conclude?
If the origin story of the Christian faith were invented to build a movement, what kind of origin story would produce the most credibility in a first-century Jewish audience?
How does the story we actually have compare to that expectation?
